sections.title: Cap and form
sections.text: Clitopilus prunulus (Scop.) P. Kumm., in the family Entolomataceae, is commonly called the Miller. Its fleshy, fragile cap is white to pale grey, matt and finely pruinose, usually 3–12 cm across. It begins convex, then flattens and becomes depressed at the centre; the margin is often inrolled when young and becomes wavy or irregular.

sections.title: Gills, stem and identifying characters
sections.text: The gills are crowded, thin and distinctly decurrent, running down the stem. They start white and become pink to salmon-pink as the spores mature. The white stem is short and sometimes curved or off-centre; it has no ring or volva. The white, tender flesh is fragile and has a strong fresh-flour smell. The spore print is pink to pinkish-brown, and the spores have longitudinal ridges.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: It grows on soil in woodland clearings, grassy places and edges, among mosses, in both broadleaf and conifer woods; it has also been recorded in pastures and along paths. In western Europe it is found mainly in summer and autumn. Its nutritional mode is discussed in the literature as saprotrophic or possibly mycorrhizal, so it should not be described as tied to a particular tree.

sections.title: Lookalikes and caution
sections.text: Some toxic white Clitocybe species can also have a pale cap and decurrent gills, but their spore print is white. A more deceptive confusion is the poisonous Livid Entoloma (Entoloma sinuatum), which has caused poisonings in France after being mistaken for the Miller: it can also smell farinaceous and produce a pinkish spore print, but is generally more robust and its gills are notched near the stem rather than strongly decurrent. Spore colour or smell alone cannot identify a mushroom safely.

traits: Fleshy, fragile, white to pale-grey matt-pruinose cap, usually 3–12 cm; convex then flattened and depressed at the centre, often with a wavy margin
Crowded, thin, strongly decurrent gills, white at first then pink when mature
Short white stem, sometimes curved or off-centre; no ring or volva
Fragile, tender white flesh with a strong fresh-flour smell
Pink to pinkish-brown spore print; spores with longitudinal ridges
On soil in clearings, grassy places and woodland edges in broadleaf or conifer woods; mainly summer and autumn in western Europe
safetyNote: Some mycological lists classify this species as edible, but toxic white Clitocybe species and especially the Livid Entoloma (Entoloma sinuatum) can be confused with it. The latter can also have a farinaceous smell and pinkish spore print, so spore colour alone is not a safety test. Never eat a wild mushroom based on this page or an image; have any collection checked by a competent mushroom expert.
